Sourcing Parts, Service, Training, and Test Equipment

Unit 2: Procurement, Contracts, and the Asset Lifecycle. Lesson 10 of 60 in CHTM Academy.

A technician needs a board today. The manufacturer quotes $4,200 with a two-week lead time. A third-party supplier quotes $1,900 overnight, and a broker has one for $700 with no warranty. The device is a ventilator. The purchase is yours to approve, and so is the consequence.

The sourcing options and their risks

Source            What you gain                  What you risk
Manufacturer      correct part, warranty,        highest price, longest lead
                  documented traceability        time
Third-party       lower price, often faster      verify quality, warranty, and
supplier                                          traceability before you buy
Refurbished       much lower price on            unknown history; ask what was
                  assemblies                      replaced and what is warranted
Exchange or       lowest cost on repairable      you owe the core back, and
core exchange     assemblies, fast                downtime if the core is lost
Broker or         availability when nothing      no warranty, no traceability,
surplus           else exists                     counterfeit exposure

Three risks run through all of it. Quality: a part that is not what the label says puts a patient behind it. Warranty: an uncovered part that fails twice costs more than the manufacturer's price. Counterfeit and regulatory exposure: a part with no traceable origin in a life-support device is a finding waiting to happen, and in the case above the right answer is the supplier who can document what the part is, not the cheapest line on the page.

Parts inventory management

Stock what the schedule and the failure history say you will need, not what feels safe. Set stock levels and reorder points per item from consumption data, keep PM kits ordered before the month they are needed, and measure turns so the shelf does not become a museum. Consignment stock sits on your shelf and is owned by the vendor until you use it, which protects cash and shifts the obsolescence risk, provided somebody reconciles it. Remember the overhead: raising one purchase order carries roughly $100 of hospital cost, so many small orders can waste more than the lower part price ever saved. Consolidate.

Sourcing service, training, and test equipment

For service, price the manufacturer, independent service organizations, and your own staff over the same years, and ask every outside provider for qualification and training records before the first visit. For training, start with the maker of the device, then price independent trainers, who are often cheaper and sometimes teach more, and negotiate the seats into the purchase while there is leverage. For test equipment, buy against the inventory you actually support: safety analyzers, simulators, meters, and gas and flow analyzers matched to the devices on the floor. Then buy the calibration with it, on a schedule, traceable to the national standards kept by NIST, with certificates on file. Test equipment out of calibration invalidates every record made with it.

Purchasing policy compliance

Follow the hospital's own rules, every time, in this order: a written specification, the number of quotes the policy requires at the dollar value, the approvals the policy requires, a purchase order raised before the work or the goods arrive, receiving confirmed against the order, and the invoice matched to both before it is approved. Sole-source purchases need a written justification. A verbal order that bypasses a purchase order leaves the hospital holding an unapproved commitment, and leaves you explaining it to an auditor.

Exam tip: compare sources on quality, warranty, traceability, and lead time, not on price alone, and never put an untraceable part in a life-support device. Buy calibration with test equipment and keep it traceable to NIST. Follow the purchasing policy's quote, approval, purchase order, and receiving sequence, and remember a purchase order carries about $100 of overhead.
Remember
Parts, service, training, and test equipment are sourced on quality, warranty, traceability, and lead time rather than price alone, inside the hospital's quote, approval, purchase order, and receiving policy.
Deeper explanation

Sourcing Parts, Service, Training, and Test Equipment, explained slowly

One part, five sources, one decision

A ventilator blower assembly. The device is life support and the hospital owns nine of them.

Source          Price    Lead      Warranty   Traceability        Decision
Manufacturer    4,200    14 days   12 months  full, documented    acceptable
Third-party     1,900    1 day     6 months   supplier will       acceptable with
supplier                                       document origin     the documentation
                                               and test records    on file
Refurbished     1,450    3 days    90 days    states what was     acceptable only
assembly                                       replaced            with the report
Exchange unit   1,100    2 days    6 months   full, core owed     best value if the
                                               back                core is returned
Broker, surplus   700    1 day     none       none                refuse

The broker's part is the cheapest line on the page and the only one that is not a candidate, because this is life support and nothing documents what the part is. Price is the last column you read on a critical device, not the first.

Setting stock levels from consumption

Item              Used    Lead     Reorder   Stock   Turns   Reading
                  /year   time     point     held    /year
Pump cassettes      240   3 days      12        30     8.0   healthy
Monitor batteries    96   7 days      10        24     4.0   healthy
Blower assemblies     3  14 days       1         1     3.0   correct: one on
                                                              the shelf
ECG module            1  21 days       0         4    0.25   overstocked; four
                                                              years of supply
Obsolete sensor       0   n/a          0         7     0.0   write it off and
                                                              free the shelf

Turns is annual usage divided by stock held. A low turn number is money sitting on a shelf becoming obsolete. The ECG module line is the common error: a technician ordered four during a bad month five years ago and nobody looked again.

The purchase order overhead, demonstrated

Approach                        Orders  Part cost  Overhead  Total
Order each item as it is          26      3,180     2,600    5,780
needed, roughly $100 per order
Consolidate into a monthly        12      3,180     1,200    4,380
order
Consolidate into a quarterly       4      3,180       400    3,580
PM kit order

Nothing changed about the parts. Consolidation saved $2,200 of hospital overhead, which is more than most negotiated part discounts return.

Test equipment and calibration

Test equipment         Matched to                  Calibration
Electrical safety      every line-powered device   annually, traceable to the
analyzer                                           national standards kept by NIST
Patient simulators     monitors, defibrillators,   annually; certificates on file
                       pumps
Gas and flow           ventilators, anesthesia     annually, plus a verification
analyzers              machines                    after transport
Pressure and           pressure transducers,       annually
vacuum meters          suction
Electrosurgical        electrosurgical units       annually
analyzer

Calibration is bought with the instrument, on a schedule, with certificates retained. A reading taken with an out-of-calibration analyzer invalidates the record it produced, which can mean re-testing a fleet and explaining it to a surveyor.

The purchasing policy sequence

1  Written specification          what is being bought, to what standard
2  Quotes                         the number the policy requires at this value
3  Sole source justification      in writing, where only one source exists
4  Approvals                      every signature the policy requires, in order
5  Purchase order                 raised before the goods or the work arrive
6  Receiving                      goods checked against the order, documented
7  Invoice matching               invoice against order against receiving
8  Payment approval               only when all three agree and the service
                                  report is in the CMMS

A verbal order skips steps 4 to 6 and leaves the hospital with a commitment nobody approved. That is the audit finding, not the price.

What to memorize

Source risks        quality, warranty, traceability, counterfeit exposure
Life support        never an untraceable part
Turns               annual usage / stock held; low turns is dead money
Consignment         vendor-owned until used; reconcile it
Purchase order      roughly $100 of overhead each; consolidate
Calibration         annual, traceable to NIST, certificates on file
Policy sequence     specification, quotes, approvals, order, receiving, match
